weekLabel: Week 3 · Meeting A · Decisions and Functions · Full Source Deck

slides.title: Turn design criteria into inspectable program logic
slides.subtitle: Booleans, comparisons, branches, loops, functions, and bounded architectural claims
slides.teaching: This is the full 82-minute source deck. The instructor may hide or skip slides at delivery time; the distributed file preserves every authored explanation and example.

slides.title: A design rule is a model of a decision
slides.statement: A conditional turns evidence into different program actions—but only according to the rule we wrote.
slides.supporting: The program can apply a criterion consistently. The designer remains responsible for the criterion, boundary, exceptions, and interpretation.
slides.teaching: Distinguish screening from approval. A pass/fail output may represent only one criterion among many.

outcomes.head: Recognize
outcomes.body: Read Boolean values and comparisons as evidence about one criterion.

outcomes.head: Branch
outcomes.body: Use if and else to produce bounded alternative actions.

outcomes.head: Test
outcomes.body: Predict below, equal, and above-boundary outcomes before running code.

outcomes.head: Package
outcomes.body: Define, call, and explain a small function that returns reusable evidence.

slides.teaching: Explain that the primer deliberately stops before loops and compound rules; those are introduced and practiced live on Wednesday.
Preview a focused progression from one value, to one decision, to one reusable procedure. Students will add repetition in the live studio.

slides.title: One threshold becomes a reusable schedule-screening procedure

tiers.task: Evaluate 39.9, 40.0, and 40.1 against an 'at least 40.0 m²' criterion.
Screen [35.0, 40.0, 62.5, 44.2, 28.0] and count values meeting the criterion.
Apply one tested area-and-daylight screen to three cases: (39.9, True), (40.0, True), (45.0, False).

slides.teaching: Explain the cumulative dependency: a loop repeats a comparison, an accumulator summarizes it, and a function centralizes the policy. The handout repeats the same ladder in Spyder.

slides.title: A defensible rule has four parts

steps.label: EVIDENCE
steps.head: What is measured?
steps.body: Area, width, ratio, count, category, or another explicit input.

steps.label: CRITERION
steps.head: What test applies?
steps.body: A comparison with a threshold, range, membership, or combination.

steps.label: ACTION
steps.head: What should code do?
steps.body: Print, record, classify, calculate, or request review.

steps.label: LIMIT
steps.head: What remains outside?
steps.body: Context, quality, exceptions, uncertainty, and human decision.

slides.teaching: Use a 40 m² program minimum. Ask where equality belongs and what the rule cannot judge.

slides.title: Recall: a Boolean answers one yes/no question
slides.definition: Recall from Week 2A: a value of type bool — a Boolean — is one of exactly two truth values, True or False. Capitalization matters. A Boolean is evidence about one question; it is not yet a decision, and not yet an action.

example.head: has_daylight = True
example.body:
Architectural questions that produce Boolean evidence:

Is the area at least 40 m²?
Is the material exterior-rated?
Does the room have daylight?

slides.note: Quotation marks change the meaning: 'True' is text, not a Boolean. Only True and False — capitalized and unquoted — are bool values.
slides.teaching: Recall from Week 2A (same light-switch analogy)—students should name it, not relearn it. Move quickly to the architectural questions; compound rules using and/or/not arrive Wednesday. Adapted from FS25 L3 slide 21, L4 slides 11–12, and L7 slides 2–3.

slides.title: Recall: a comparison creates Boolean evidence
slides.code:
area_m2 = 44.2
minimum_m2 = 40.0
meets_minimum = area_m2 >= minimum_m2

print(meets_minimum)
slides.explainBody: Recall from Week 2A: a comparison expression evaluates two values and returns True or False. It records evidence about one criterion; it does not yet determine a message or action.
slides.teaching: Recall from Week 2A slide 27, same code and threshold—students should name it, not relearn it. Test 39.9, 40.0, and 40.1 to establish the boundary, then move quickly to the conditional that finally acts on this evidence.

slides.title: Recall: comparison operators translate different questions
slides.callout: Recall from Week 2A: every comparison returns True or False. = assigns a value; == compares two values.
slides.teaching: Recall from Week 2A's operator table (same six operators)—students should name it, not relearn it. Adapted from FS25 L7 slide 5 and Lxx Operator slide 7. Students say each comparison aloud before running it.

slides.title: A conditional chooses which block of code runs
slides.definition: A conditional statement uses a Boolean condition to decide whether a block of code runs. Python gives you if for the first case, else for everything that remains, and elif for cases in between.

example.head: if area_m2 >= minimum_m2:
example.body: The condition is any expression that evaluates to True or False. When it is True the indented block runs. When it is False Python skips that whole block and continues below it.

slides.note: Ordinary code runs every line from top to bottom. A conditional is the first structure that lets Python skip lines entirely.
slides.teaching: Adapted from FS25 L8 slides 2, 5, and 6. Contrast ordinary top-to-bottom execution with a branch that may be skipped, then read the line part by part on the next slide.

slides.title: Every if line carries the same five parts

parts.label: The keyword
parts.body: Announces that a decision starts here.

parts.label: At least
parts.body: Includes the boundary value. Plain > would reject 40.0.

parts.label: The threshold
parts.body: Named once, so the policy is visible and easy to change.

parts.label: The colon
parts.body: Opens the indented block that runs when True.

slides.teaching: Point at each numbered part in turn and have students say it aloud: keyword, evidence, operator, threshold, colon. Ask which single character students are most likely to forget, then show the SyntaxError that follows a missing colon.

slides.title: if executes a block only when its condition is true
slides.code:
area_m2 = 44.2
minimum_m2 = 40.0

if area_m2 >= minimum_m2:
    print('meets area criterion')
slides.explainHead: Colon and indentation define the block
slides.explainBody: The condition follows if and ends with a colon. Indented statements belong to the branch. When the condition is False, the block is skipped.
slides.teaching: Point to the condition, colon, indentation, and controlled statement. Then run with 35 m².

slides.title: Read a conditional as evidence, policy, and action

left.head: Python structure

right.head: Architectural reading
right.body:
Evidence: room area
Policy: area ≥ 40 m²
Action: mark this criterion as met
Limit: no claim about overall room quality

slides.teaching: Have students annotate one conditional with these four labels.

slides.title: Commit to an answer before Python gives you one
slides.code:
area_m2 = 35.0
minimum_m2 = 40.0

if area_m2 >= minimum_m2:
    status = 'meets criterion'
else:
    status = 'review area'

print(status)
slides.question: What does this print?
slides.why: 35.0 >= 40.0 is False, so only the else branch runs. print shows a string's characters, not its quotes.
slides.teaching: Make everyone commit before revealing. A is chosen by students who read >= as 'is 35 near 40' or assume the first branch always runs. C assumes print shows the quotation marks that appear in the code. D assumes print(status) reports the comparison rather than the text that was assigned. Reveal the answer strip, then run the same code on the next slide.

slides.title: else makes the alternative action explicit
slides.code:
area_m2 = 35.0
minimum_m2 = 40.0

if area_m2 >= minimum_m2:
    status = 'meets criterion'
else:
    status = 'review area'

print(status)
slides.explainBody: if handles True; else handles every remaining case. The two messages should describe evidence and required review without overstating design quality.
slides.teaching: This is the reveal for the previous predict slide. Ask whether 'bad room' would be a defensible else message. Replace it with bounded language.

slides.title: If/else routes one question to two explicit actions
slides.teaching: Trace only one route at a time. Emphasize that the diagram records a criterion result, not an overall design approval.

slides.title: The boundary is a policy choice, not a Python default
rows: below the minimum on either rule
above the minimum on either rule
slides.callout: Write the expected column before you run the code. 'At least 40 m²' means >=. Choosing > silently rejects a room that exactly meets the requirement.
slides.teaching: Only the middle row separates the two operators, and that row is the whole policy argument. Ask which operator matches the words in the program brief, then keep this table on screen for the closing exercise.

slides.title: elif represents more than two meaningful ranges
slides.explainBody: Conditions are checked from top to bottom. The first true branch runs and the rest are skipped. Put the most restrictive relevant threshold first.
slides.teaching: Reverse the first two thresholds and ask why 30 would be classified incorrectly.

slides.title: Logical operators combine Boolean questions
rows: Are area AND daylight criteria met?
at least one condition is True
slides.callout: Write compound conditions in words first. Parentheses make grouping and policy visible.
slides.teaching: Adapted from FS25 L7 slide 6. Keep short-circuit evaluation as an optional verbal extension.

slides.title: Compound rules combine Boolean evidence

left.head: AND
left.body: A and B is True only when both are True. Use when all stated criteria must be satisfied.

right.head: OR and NOT
right.body: A or B is True when either is True. not A reverses a Boolean. Parentheses make compound intent visible.

slides.teaching: Use egress width and travel-distance criteria. Ask whether the policy requires both or either.

slides.title: and requires both criteria to pass
slides.code:
area_m2 = 44.2
has_daylight = True

ready_for_review = (
    area_m2 >= 40.0
    and has_daylight
)
print(ready_for_review)
slides.explainBody: Parentheses make the grouping readable across lines. The Boolean name should describe exactly what the rule supports—not imply final design approval.
slides.teaching: Test all four combinations of criterion True/False and daylight True/False.

slides.title: Boundary cases define the policy
slides.callout: Write expected results before execution. Boundaries are policy decisions, not Python defaults.
slides.teaching: Students identify which row would change if the operator were > rather than >=.

slides.title: A loop repeats a block of code

left.head: Definition
left.body:
A loop is a control structure that executes the same indented block repeatedly. A for loop—used all course—visits each item in a sequence, once per item.

A while loop instead repeats only while a condition stays True, for example (shown for contrast only, not used further this semester):
count = 0
while count < 3:
    count += 1

right.head: Why use one
right.body:
Apply one tested rule consistently
Avoid copied calculations
Process several rooms or options
Summarize repeated results

slides.teaching: Adapted from FS25 L8 slides 11, 13, 14, and 25. The course begins with for because room records form a known sequence. The while example is illustrative contrast only—do not imply it received the same practice as for; no while exercise follows.

slides.title: Repetition should preserve one tested rule
slides.statement: A loop applies the same operation to several items without copying the code block.
slides.supporting: Write and test the rule on one record first. Then repeat it and inspect whether each iteration uses the intended item.
slides.teaching: Contrast repeating a tested operation with copy-pasting several slightly different versions.

slides.title: A for loop visits each item in an ordered collection
slides.explainHead: A list, then the loop variable
slides.explainBody: A list is an ordered collection of values, written in square brackets and separated by commas—room_areas_m2 = [35.0, 62.5, 44.2] holds three areas in order. On each iteration, area_m2 refers to the next list item, and the indented block runs once per item.
slides.teaching: Trace the loop variable through three iterations before running.

slides.title: An accumulator summarizes repeated results
slides.explainBody: Initialize before the loop. Update inside the conditional block. Inspect after the loop. A wrong indentation can reset or report the count at the wrong time.
slides.teaching: Use a trace table with iteration, area, comparison result, and passing_count.

slides.title: Loop structure reveals where state changes

left.head: Outside the loop
left.body:
Inputs and initial state

Final reporting after all items are processed

right.head: Inside the loop
right.body:
Current item
Per-item comparison
Per-item output
Accumulator update

slides.teaching: Show how indentation determines whether an action happens once or once per room.

slides.title: A function is a named reusable procedure

steps.label: INPUT
steps.head: Receive arguments
steps.body: Parameters name the values needed for the task.

steps.label: PROCESS
steps.head: Run instructions
steps.body: The indented body calculates or applies a rule.

steps.label: RETURN
steps.head: Send a result back
steps.body: The caller can store, compare, test, or display it.

slides.teaching: Adapted from FS25 L10 slides 2–6. Use the machine analogy: inputs enter, instructions operate, and a result leaves.

slides.title: Function definition and call are separate
slides.code:
def rectangular_area(length_m, width_m):
    area_m2 = length_m * width_m
    return area_m2

gallery_area = rectangular_area(8.5, 5.2)
print(gallery_area)
slides.explainBody: def creates the function. Parameters name required inputs. The body performs the procedure. return sends one result back to the calling code.
slides.teaching: Trace definition, call, parameter values, local result, return value, and assignment. Read the def line the same way as the if line earlier: keyword, name, parameters, colon, indented block.

slides.title: A function is a small tested contract

steps.label: NAME
steps.head: State the purpose
steps.body: Use a verb or precise noun phrase describing one coherent responsibility.

steps.label: INPUT
steps.head: Define parameters
steps.body: Name required quantities, meanings, and units.

steps.label: RETURN
steps.head: Produce a result
steps.body: Return evidence that later code can store, compare, visualize, or test.

steps.label: TEST
steps.head: Check the contract
steps.body: Use known, boundary, and invalid cases.

slides.teaching: Ask whether a function called calculate_everything has a clear contract. Prefer smaller responsibilities.

slides.title: A function is a reusable evidence machine

steps.label: RULE
steps.head: Apply one tested policy
steps.body: Compare the two values once, in one place.

steps.label: RETURN
steps.head: Produce data
steps.body: Return True or False; do not hide it in print().

steps.label: REUSE
steps.head: Call with new cases
steps.body: Test below, equal, and above the boundary.

slides.teaching: Connect the function box to the handout's three boundary cases. The same rule should give predictable results for every call.

slides.title: return provides data; print displays text
slides.code:
def rectangular_area(length_m, width_m):
    return length_m * width_m

area_m2 = rectangular_area(8.5, 5.2)
print(f'Area: {area_m2:.1f} m²')
print(area_m2 >= 40.0)
slides.explainBody: The function returns a numerical value. Calling code decides how to store, format, compare, or visualize it. Printing inside every function would reduce reuse.
slides.teaching: Ask why the returned float is more useful later than one preformatted sentence.

slides.title: Default arguments make a stated assumption visible
slides.explainBody: A default is used when the caller omits that argument. It should be documented, justified, and easy to override. Formatting may control display, but not model validity.
slides.teaching: Ask whether a universal 10% allowance is defensible and when a required argument would be safer.

slides.title: A function can return more than two answers
slides.output:
review area
meets area criterion
generous area
slides.explainHead: Same rule shape, one more branch
slides.explainBody: elif inside a function works exactly like elif on its own — the function just returns evidence language instead of printing it, so the SAME tested rule can be reused anywhere in the script without retyping the thresholds.
slides.teaching: Ask what changes if generous_m2 were lowered to 60.0 — which room's classification flips?

slides.title: Apply one tested function to the full room schedule
slides.code:
room_areas_m2 = [35.0, 62.5, 44.2, 78.0,
                 28.5, 55.0, 40.0, 18.0]

for area_m2 in room_areas_m2:
    print(area_m2, area_tier(area_m2))
slides.output:
35.0 review area
62.5 meets area criterion
44.2 meets area criterion
78.0 generous area
28.5 review area
55.0 meets area criterion
40.0 meets area criterion
18.0 review area
slides.explainBody: The loop supplies every record to the same tested function. Office at exactly 40.0 reaches 'meets area criterion' because the function includes equality.
slides.teaching: Trace the first, fourth, and seventh records. Ask which single function line controls the 40.0 boundary.

slides.title: Count the schedule and verify that every room was classified
slides.explainBody: Expected counts are 3 review, 4 meets, and 1 generous. The assertion proves that all eight records landed in exactly one tier; it does not prove the policy is sufficient for design approval.
slides.teaching: Have students hand-count the three groups before revealing 3, 4, and 1. Then explain what the final assertion checks and what it cannot check.

slides.title: Translate one room criterion into tested logic
slides.prompt: Screen room area against a 40 m² minimum without calling the room good or bad.
steps: Write the evidence, criterion, action, and limitation.
Write a function returning bounded status text.
Call the function three times and compare each result with your prediction.
slides.teaching: Expected: 39.9 fails, 40.0 and 40.1 pass. Review >=, Boolean values, indentation, return values, and repeated calls. Bounded language might say 'meets area criterion' rather than 'approved.' Limitations can include daylight quality, accessibility, egress, proportion, or program fit.

slides.title: A small rule can already be inspectable
takeaways: if/else connects evidence to bounded actions.
Boundary cases reveal a policy choice.
Functions package a reusable procedure; Wednesday adds loops and compound rules.
slides.teaching: Exit ticket: students write one architectural rule and its most important boundary case. Tell them to bring that rule to the live Spyder studio.
